director.chapterArc: A survivalist crisis where Jab's magical ability fails, forcing him into exhaustion and panic before discovering a new rule of detachment that saves his brother.
director.restraintNote: Maintain clinical precision during the failure sequence; do not dramatize the physical cost until the realization phase. The horror is in the silence after the coughing fit, not the sound itself.

cues.delivery: Jab's realization of total depletion. The tone is flat but heavy with the weight of a man who has run out of options.
cues.from: Jab put his hand on his brother's chest and felt the heat coming up through the blanket into his palm like a stone left in a fire, and he understood, quite calmly, that he had come to the end of what he had.
cues.through: And he had a piece of river metal at his throat that could cut through anything in the fir stand and could not touch what was in his brother's leg.
cues.reason: Shift from narrative description to internal crisis; Jab accepts he cannot fix this.

cues.delivery: Jab's decision to try the impossible. The voice is flat and functional, like counting fish.
cues.from: Instead he put it out and let the metal come back and lie against his sternum where it belonged, and went and knelt by his brother again, and said, out loud, in the flat voice he used for counting fish:
cues.reason: Transition from failed magic to desperate theory; Jab speaks as if reciting a protocol.

cues.delivery: The physical cost of the failed attempt. The narration slows to emphasize the coldness and heaviness spreading through Jab's body.
cues.from: And it did cost. That was the part he had not expected, because nothing had happened and he could not see how nothing could be expensive. But somewhere in the middle of it a coldness started up behind his eyes, and his hands went heavy, and the small warmth under his breastbone thinned out like a fire with too much on it — and he knew that feeling, he had known it since he was fourteen and had tried to hold the blade for a whole afternoon on the jam to prove he could. That was the bottom of it. That was what it felt like when a person spent what they had.
cues.through: He kept going past it anyway, because his brother was making that sound.
cues.reason: Jab realizes he has spent his reserves for nothing; a moment of pure exhaustion.

cues.delivery: The coughing fit and Jab's delayed reaction. The pacing must feel disjointed to mirror the 'three heartbeats' of delay.
cues.from: Jab was two arm's-lengths from him and it took him three heartbeats to get there.
cues.through: He had never in his life had that happen. He had always simply been where he needed to be, fast, without the between part; his body had done that for him since he was nine years old on a slick bar with fish coming in. This time he came up off his knees and the world went sideways and gray, and he had to put a hand down on the ground and wait for it, three whole beats, listening to his brother not breathe.
cues.reason: Jab fails his own reflex; a moment where he is not in control.

cues.delivery: Jab's self-reprimand. The voice is dry and logical, stripping away emotion to fix the mistake.
cues.from: Best part of an hour, he thought. He had spent the best part of an hour of the worst night they had had, pushing at a door, while the fire went down and his brother lay flat.
cues.through: He meant it about as much as a man means anything at that hour. But he made himself say the whole of it out loud, to fix it: "You don't get to try things on him. You try them on you, or you don't try them."
cues.reason: Jab establishes a new rule for himself; he speaks to his own limitations.

cues.delivery: The discovery of the 'slope' sensation. The tone is observational and detached, treating it as a physical fact rather than magic.
cues.from: Something answered. It was not a voice and it was not a picture. It was closer to the feeling of a slope under your feet in the dark: a sense of which way the ground went.
cues.reason: Jab identifies the mechanism; he treats the supernatural like weather.

cues.delivery: The formulation of the rule. Jab speaks with clarity and finality; this is a survival tactic.
cues.from: "So don't ask it when you want an answer," he said. "Ask it when you don't care."
cues.through: That was a rule he could actually use, and it was the first useful thing he had got out of the entire night.
cues.reason: Jab crystallizes his new understanding into a usable principle.

cues.delivery: The successful application of the rule. The pacing is efficient and immediate; Jab acts before he thinks.
cues.from: He was not thinking about the fever at all. He was breaking the shelter down in the dark, working by feel, coiling the hide cords, and he came past his brother to lift him, and as he got his arms in under him something in the middle of Jab's chest said, quite plainly and with no encouragement at all: here it comes.
cues.through: Ninety seconds later Tonk went rigid and made the sound, and the bad wave came through him, and Jab was already there with his hand where it needed to be — not beginning to get there, not reaching, already there — and it went through and it went past, and it was over faster than any of them had been in a week.
cues.reason: Jab anticipates the seizure without panic; a shift from failure to competence.

cues.delivery: Jab's questioning of the power. The tone is weary and curious; he asks a question to which there is no answer.
cues.from: He sat back on his heels in the dark, and put his hand flat on his own breastbone, over the metal, over the small stubborn warmth that had been there for four years and had never once done anything he had not asked it to.
cues.through: It did not tell him. It sat there being warm, the way it had while he split fish and cut willow and hauled logs and lit a blade over a log jam, the way it had been while his parents went down the river in the dark and he lay on a gravel slope with his brother's blood on his hands and could not do one single thing about any of it.
cues.reason: The realization that the power does not heal; it only senses.

pauses.after: This one did not let go.
pauses.reason: Scene turn: The bad hour has failed to end. A moment of dread before the description continues.
Emphasis on the terrifying calmness of Jab's realization.

pauses.after: And he had a piece of river metal at his throat that could cut through anything in the fir stand and could not touch what was in his brother's leg.
pauses.reason: Emotional landing: Jab realizes his tools are useless against this specific threat.
Highlighting the irrational impulse before he stops himself.
Speaker reset/Thought break: Jab speaks a decision aloud to solidify it.
Emphasis on the unexpected physical toll of the failed magic.

pauses.reason: Emotional landing: The cost of the failed attempt is fully realized; silence needed for exhaustion.
Highlighting the critical delay in Jab's reaction time.

He had always simply been where he needed to be, fast, without the between part; his body had done that for him since he was nine years old on a slick bar with fish coming in. This time he came up off his knees and the world went sideways and gray, and he had to put a hand down on the ground and wait for it, three whole beats, listening to his brother not breathe.
pauses.reason: Major emotional landing/Scene turn: Jab realizes his reflexes have failed him. A long pause to let the horror sink in.

pauses.reason: Speaker reset: Jab finishes his self-reprimand and moves into observation mode.

pauses.after: Wrong. He sat with that. He had been right twice and wrong once, and a person who had been right twice and wrong once knew nothing at all yet; he had watched his aunt's daughter guess the weather for a whole summer at better odds than that.
pauses.reason: Emotional landing: The realization that he was wrong because of bias. A moment of intellectual reckoning.
The moment Jab's internal warning triggers; a sharp pivot in the narrative flow.
